articles.title: AI’s Frontier Faces Calls for Safety Slowdown
articles.summary: Bloomberg’s Ed Ludlow breaks down calls from AI for a slower pace at the frontier, arguing safety needs time to catch up with increasingly powerful models. The debate is reaching Washington and Wall Street, with AI-linked stocks under pressure as investors weigh what slower development means for the spending boom. (Source: Bloomberg)

articles.title: AI Slowdown Fears Shake Wall Street
articles.summary: Get a jump start on the US trading day with Dani Burger and Isabelle Lee on "Bloomberg Open Interest." Tech stocks slide as new warnings call for slowing the AI race, while Wall Street braces for the Fed with inflation raising the stakes. Nissan's Christian Meunier says US auto tariffs were tough to navigate at first, but it helped the company expand its US footprint. Plus, Canada’s Prime Minister Mark Carney on reviving US trade talks. Barclays CEO C.S. Venkatakrishnan on the forces squeezing global bond markets. And former DeepMind scientist Alex Turner on AI safety, while Nancy Tengler explains why the sell-off could be a buying opportunity. (Source: Bloomberg)

articles.title: What Blockchain Still Needs to Win Wall Street
articles.summary: Kaiko CEO Ambre Soubiran joins Bloomberg Open Interest to explain why blockchain adoption on Wall Street is taking longer than expected. She argues the technology is ready, but tokenized markets still need trusted data, risk controls and traditional market safeguards before 24/7 trading and instant settlement can scale. (Source: Bloomberg)

articles.title: The Post-SaaS Architecture: How a $14,000/month AWS bill for 35 req/sec cured our team of cloud delusions
articles.summary: A few months ago, I was brought in to audit the infrastructure of a post-Series A fintech company that was bleeding cash. The leadership team couldn't understand why their monthly Amazon Web Services bill was hovering around $14,200 while their actual traffic—measured at the edge—peaked at roughly 35 requests per second during business hours. Thirty-five. That is not a typo. That’s about 2,100 requests a minute. A single Raspberry Pi 4 running a bare-bones Go HTTP server could handle that workload while sitting on a kitchen table without breaking into a sweat. articles.author: Marcus Vane
